evidence_quotes.quote: In this paper we compare the contracts of two Portuguese utilities with different governance models: a public–private partnership and a public–public partnership.

Therefore, the comparison between different models seems of paramount importance, so as to understand the way they ‘behave’ in terms of risk and performance management: the former, linked to mitigation and allocation of ‘project’ risks; the latter related to the existing incentives and the consequences that might arise.
The PUP entity analyzed is AdRA, and was created under a partnership contract signed in 2009 between the central government and several municipalities.

Regarding the sunshine regulation carried out by ERSAR, AdVouga enjoys the highest qualitative evaluation in most indicators, except in the average collection period (ﬁnancial) indicator in which it achieved the ‘average’ qualitative level, and in the cost recovery ratio (operator sustainability) where it achieved the ‘unsatisfactory’ level

Indeed, when it comes to introducing appropriate incentives to operator efﬁciency and service quality, as well as effective risk allocation between the public authority, operator, and end-users, the devil is in the detail of the contractual mechanisms introduced and their rigorous enforcement.

criterion_notes.c1: Does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access. Aside from brief national background statistics from ERSAR (95% water and 81% wastewater coverage in Portugal), the study investigates principal-agent contracting practices, risk allocation, and operator performance management in one retail public-public partnership (AdRA) and one wholesale bulk water public-private partnership (AdVouga).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — examines institutional, contractual, and regulatory governance factors (public-public partnership vs. contractual public-private partnership models, concession/management contract clauses, tariff-review formulas, and ERSAR regulatory oversight). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — although utility ownership structures and cost-recovery tariff rules are discussed, the contractual mechanisms analyzed govern principal-agent risk allocation, guaranteed shareholder returns, municipal rent payments, wholesale bulk pricing, and operator financial monitoring rather than rules directly governing household or community service access (eligibility, connection, affordability, or disconnection). Note: even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study is still excluded because it fails Criteria 1 and 4.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains empirical qualitative case-study evidence comparing primary contract provisions, viability-study financial schedules, risk-allocation matrices, employee labor-contract data (2010-2011 for AdRA), and ERSAR regulatory evaluation indicators for two Portuguese water utilities (AdRA and AdVouga).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports no outcome relevant to household or community access, connection, service availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion. Reported outcomes are limited to contractual risk-sharing and shareholder return provisions, employee contract types (AdRA), wholesale bulk volumetric tariffs charged to a municipal association (AdVouga), and operator-level ERSAR financial and parametric water-quality ratings (average collection period, operator cost-recovery ratio, and 100% parametric water quality compliance).
criterion_notes.c5: The study design (comparative case study), unit of analysis and sample (two Portuguese water utilities/contracts: AdRA and AdVouga), exposure (PUP vs. cPPP governance and contract design), and utility/contract-level outcomes are clearly identifiable from the full text, although no eligible household/community service-access outcome is measured.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English, an eligible language without translation.

study_design: Comparative qualitative case study (contract and institutional analysis of two water utility partnerships)
population_and_sample: Two Portuguese water utility partnerships (unit of analysis: utility/contract): Águas da Região de Aveiro (AdRA, a retail water and wastewater public–public partnership between the central state and 10 municipalities) and Águas do Vouga (AdVouga, a bulk water supply contractual public–private partnership serving an association of municipalities, AMCV)
exposure: Utility governance and contracting model: public–public partnership (PUP) management contract vs. contractual public–private partnership (cPPP) concession contract (including tariff-adjustment, cost-recovery, risk-allocation, and monitoring clauses)
outcome: Contractual risk allocation, tariff-review and shareholder return provisions, operator employee labor contract composition (AdRA, 2010–2011), bulk water wholesale price and investment schedules, and ERSAR operator financial and water-quality sunshine ratings (average collection period, cost recovery ratio, and parametric water quality compliance for AdVouga); no household or community access, connection, continuity, affordability, or exclusion outcomes reported
rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome). This comparative case study analyzes the partnership and concession contracts of two Portuguese water utilities—AdRA (a retail water/wastewater public–public partnership) and AdVouga (a wholesale bulk water contractual public–private partnership)—focusing on principal–agent contract design, financial risk allocation, shareholder return rules, staff employment contract shares, wholesale bulk water pricing, and operator-level ERSAR financial and water-quality sunshine ratings. It does not examine household or community water/sanitation service access (c1 = no) and reports no outcome measuring access, connection, availability, continuity/reliability, quantity, household affordability, or exclusion (c4 = no). Under both the plain wording of Criterion 2 (where the institutional/contractual focus qualifies) and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (where the analyzed contract rules govern operator-authority risk sharing rather than household service access), the study is excluded for lacking any eligible service-access outcome.
